title: Every Chair Wobbles Eventually. A Field Guide to Sitting Down on the Problem
body: The dining chair wobbled for eight months before I did anything, and the eight months were the real repair lesson. A wobble is not a defect. A wobble is a chair filing a report. Joints loosen, glue ages, wood moves with the seasons, and every chair on earth is slowly becoming a wobbly chair. The question is never whether. It is when you will read the report. Diagnosis first, tools second. A wobbly chair has exactly three possible conversations happening. One, the joint has pulled apart and the glue has let go. Two, the screw or bolt has loosened and just needs a turn. Three, the wood itself has worn, a dowel gone oval, a seat socket widened, and no amount of glue will fix geometry. Flip the chair, hold it firmly, and rock it while watching each joint. The guilty joint will show itself. It moves. Everything else is theater. The screw case is a gift. Tighten it. Done. But the glue case is where beginners go wrong, and I went wrong there myself, twice, before learning the rule that matters. Glue does not fix a loose joint. Glue fixes a fitted joint. If the tenon slides in and out freely, gluing it as-is just glues the gap in place, and the chair will wobble again with a glue skin you now have to scrape. The joint must be rebuilt tight. A shim of wood veneer, a wrap of cotton thread soaked in glue around a loose dowel, a slightly larger dowel. Restore the fit first. Then the glue has something to do. The other beginner sin is clamping impatience. Glue needs time and pressure, and the chair needs to be clamped in a position that is square, not in a position that is convenient. I once clamped a chair arm at a slight angle because that was how it sat in the clamp, and the chair cured that way, permanently leaning, like a man who fell asleep on a train. Check square with something square. Then wait the full time on the bottle, which is always longer than your enthusiasm. The third case, worn wood, is the humbling one. A chair that has been sat on hard for thirty years can have sockets you could park a marble in. The honest fixes are real but bigger. Drill out the old dowel and glue in a fresh one, slightly oversized, turned or sanded to fit. It is an hour of work and it makes the chair younger than it has been in decades, and there is a specific satisfaction in sitting on your own repair that no purchased chair will ever provide. Prevention, learned late. Chairs want their joints checked once a year, the way teeth want cleaning. Two minutes per chair, a quick rock test, and any developing movement gets a screw turn or a glue touch-in while it is still a negotiation instead of a divorce. The chairs in my house now get a checkup every spring, the same week the smoke alarm gets its battery. The repaired chair has outlived two newer chairs that came and went with the flat. There is a quiet bond with a chair you have rebuilt. You know its skeleton. When guests lean back on it and someone flinches, I do not flinch. I was in there. I know what is holding.
